past_actions.summary: Extend driving shifts — push from roughly 45 hours per week to 55-58 hours. Target airport queues, late-night Friday/Saturday surges, and stadium event windows to maximize per-hour yield.
past_actions.emotional_state: Anxious and slightly suppressed. There is a low-grade dread running underneath the surface that Robert is actively managing by staying busy. The anxiety is real but not yet loud enough to force a behavioral break. He is functional, outwardly calm to his son, inwardly cycling. Sleep is slightly disrupted — waking at 3am some nights running numbers in his head. He is not in crisis mode. He is in pre-crisis denial mode, which feels from the inside like competence.

past_actions.summary: Push driving hours to 60-62 per week for the next four weeks while the window is still open. Prioritize high-margin ride types: airport runs, late-night premium hours, and any local events. Log every dollar. The income window before RoboRide arrives is finite and I need to bank as much as possible.
past_actions.emotional_state: The denial broke. Not completely — Robert is not in free fall — but the specific combination of a company name, a city name, and a two-month timeline did something that generalized anxiety about automation could not do. It made the threat concrete. He is now operating in a different register: frightened but not frozen. The fear is functional, which is the best version of fear. He sat in a gas station parking lot for twelve minutes processing something he couldn't process while driving. He is not telling Marcus anything. He is holding the external presentation of stability very tightly. Underneath: a sustained high-stress hum, occasional intrusive calculations in the middle of the night, a specific new guilt about the brakes. He is a man who has spent six years being competent at one thing and is now staring at a horizon where that competence expires. He has not yet grieved that. He is not ready to. He is doing what he knows how to do — working — while trying, for the first time, to look sideways at what else might exist.

past_actions.summary: Apply for Maria's $2,500 workforce retraining grant this week. Not research it. Not bookmark it. Fill out the form and submit it. The council is expected to pass the program. I qualify. Waiting to apply until after it passes is the same logic that kept me from fixing the brakes — deferring a clear action because the timing feels slightly uncertain. The time to apply is now.
past_actions.emotional_state: Resolved but not calm. The difference between tick 1 and tick 2 is that the fear has found a direction. Last month the fear was ambient — it was in the walls. This month it is pointing at specific things: the grant form, the permit exam date, Carlos's phone number. Robert is not optimistic. He is not telling himself this is going to be fine. He is telling himself that there are four actions in front of him and each one is something he can actually do, and that doing them is better than not doing them, and that is enough to move on. He is still not telling Marcus anything beyond that work has been busy. The weight of carrying that alone is real. But he is not ready to explain something he hasn't resolved yet. The car payment sits in the back of his mind every time he runs the numbers — $480 on an asset that serves a market that is expiring. He has not made a decision about it yet. That decision is coming. He knows it's coming. He is not ready for it this tick.

past_actions.summary: Enroll in NEMT (Non-Emergency Medical Transport) driver certification course at Millfield Community College. Pay the $320 course registration fee this week. The course is 6 weeks, evenings only. I can keep driving daytime shifts while completing it. NEMT drivers are not being replaced by RoboRide — the liability exposure and regulatory complexity of transporting medical patients makes autonomous vehicles nonviable in that segment for the foreseeable future. This is the retrain move I identified last tick. I am done researching it. I am registering.
